script.opening: "I got back from Thailand four days ago and I feel awful — high fever, a pounding headache right behind my eyes, and aching all over, like my bones hurt. I’ve come out in a rash too. The walk-in did a malaria test and it was negative. What is it?"

facts.text: Fever started 2 days after getting back (so 2 days ago), up to 39.5 on his thermometer. Severe headache behind the eyes, worse moving his eyes. Aching muscles and joints — "like my bones hurt". Rash on his chest and arms since this morning, red and blotchy; it fades when he presses it (will show the camera).

If asked: "They did one malaria finger-prick test and a blood film, both negative, and said to see my GP." They wrote down his temperature 39.2, pulse 104, BP 118/72, oxygen 98%. No other bloods were done.

No tummy pain, not vomiting, no bleeding gums or nosebleeds, no blood in urine or stools, no black stools, no new bruising or tiny red spots. Not drowsy or confused. Drinking about 2 litres a day; passing urine normally. No breathlessness, no neck stiffness.

Three weeks backpacking: Bangkok, then rural north (Chiang Mai, jungle trekking), then the islands. Lots of mosquito bites, used repellent "sometimes". No malaria tablets — "they said Thailand was low risk". No fresh-water swimming, no animal bites. Had unprotected sex once with a fellow traveller (only if asked sensitively). No tattoos or injections abroad. Travel companion, Josh, is well.
Fit and well. Only paracetamol so far; was about to buy ibuprofen. No allergies. Had typhoid and hepatitis A jabs before travelling.
Lives with parents. Trainee accountant; due back at work tomorrow. Mum can drive him to hospital.

Flushed, tired, aching, lying on the sofa. Reassured by the negative malaria test: "So it could still be malaria?" Ask how long it will last and about work. Agree to hospital tests today once the reason is explained.

ice.ideas: "Some travel bug. The malaria test was negative, so I guessed not that."
ice.concerns: "Whether it’s serious. A girl in our hostel ended up in hospital with something." Worried about missing work in his first year of training.
ice.expectations: "To know what it is and get something to feel better — ibuprofen, probably."

cues: "The malaria test was negative" — false reassurance; one negative test does not exclude malaria.
"I was going to get ibuprofen" — NSAIDs to avoid in possible dengue.
"Behind my eyes, like my bones hurt" — classic dengue features to pick up.

checkpoints.text: Approaches FEVER IN A RETURNING TRAVELLER structurally and EXCLUDES MALARIA first — recognising a single negative film does not exclude it (three samples over 24–48 hours, UK malaria guidelines 2016 — same-day hospital assessment)
Recognises DENGUE (retro-orbital headache, severe myalgia, rash, leucopenia/thrombocytopenia, SE Asia, <2-week incubation) and confirms with RT-PCR/NS1/serology
Takes a structured TRAVEL/exposure history and constructs the differential (malaria, dengue, typhoid, hepatitis, rickettsia, leptospirosis, VHF by region, COVID)

Investigates appropriately via same-day hospital assessment (FBC, LFTs, U&E, blood films ×3, dengue NS1/serology, cultures), uses the recorded observations for a sepsis screen (NICE NG253) and ensures they are repeated at the same-day assessment, and monitors platelets/haematocrit

Recognises dengue WARNING SIGNS needing ADMISSION (critical phase as the fever settles) and manages supportively (hydration, paracetamol), AVOIDING NSAIDs/aspirin, knowing the laboratory reports confirmed dengue (clinicians notify suspected malaria/enteric fever)
Explains the returning-traveller reasoning clearly, addresses his concern, and checks understanding
Elicits and addresses his specific worries (how serious it is, time off work, infecting others), and gives clear advice on avoiding NSAIDs and aspirin and what to expect day to day

Safety-nets robustly: warning signs warranting urgent reassessment/admission (A&E or 999), same-day repeat malaria testing, and review, with advice before future travel (second infection risk) — excluding malaria and recognising severe dengue, not reassured by one negative film

worked.txt: "With a fever after travelling, my first job is always to be sure it isn’t malaria — and importantly, one negative test doesn’t fully rule it out — it needs three over a day or two — so I’m sending you to the hospital’s acute team today for repeat blood films. We don’t take chances with that."

"That said, the headache behind your eyes, the deep ‘breakbone’ aching and the rash, just back from Thailand, fit dengue — a mosquito-borne infection. They’ll send a specific test and check your blood count, as it can drop the platelets."
"Tell me more — rural or city, any prophylaxis, bites, freshwater swimming, food and water, any unwell contacts? That helps me cover the other possibilities like typhoid."

"Most dengue is self-limiting, but the trickiest time is often when the fever comes down, so watch for warning signs — bad tummy pain, persistent vomiting, any bleeding, bruising or spots, or becoming very drowsy. Those mean hospital, urgently."
"Treatment is fluids, rest and paracetamol. Crucially, AVOID ibuprofen and aspirin — they can worsen bleeding when platelets are low."

"The hospital team will repeat the malaria films today and I’ll chase the dengue test. Go straight to A&E or call 999 if any of those warning signs appear, you can’t keep fluids down, or you pass much less urine. Later on, if it is dengue, talk to a travel clinic before any trip to a dengue area, as a second infection can be more severe."

f.learning: Fever in a RETURNING TRAVELLER demands a structured approach, and MALARIA must be excluded first as the must-not-miss — a single negative film does not exclude it, so three samples over 24–48 hours are needed (UK malaria treatment guidelines 2016), which means same-day hospital assessment. DENGUE (a mosquito-borne flavivirus common in SE Asia and the tropics, incubation usually <2 weeks) presents with high fever, severe RETRO-ORBITAL headache, marked MYALGIA/arthralgia ("breakbone fever"), rash, and often leucopenia and THROMBOCYTOPENIA, confirmed by RT-PCR/NS1 antigen early or serology later (UKHSA RIPL). Take a structured travel/exposure history (where, when, rural/urban, activities, bites, prophylaxis/vaccinations, food/water, freshwater swimming, sexual/animal exposure) and build the differential (malaria, dengue, typhoid, hepatitis A, rickettsia, leptospirosis, viral haemorrhagic fever in specific regions — isolate/notify, COVID), investigating with FBC, LFTs, U&E, blood films ×3, dengue NS1/serology and cultures while monitoring platelets/haematocrit. Critically, recognise dengue WARNING SIGNS of severe dengue needing admission (WHO 2009, international) — abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, fluid accumulation, mucosal bleeding/petechiae/bruising, lethargy/restlessness, liver enlargement, rising haematocrit with rapid platelet fall — most likely in the critical phase as the fever settles (often days 3–7); screen for sepsis (NICE NG253); and manage supportively with hydration, rest and PARACETAMOL while AVOIDING NSAIDs/aspirin (bleeding/platelet risk). Laboratories report confirmed dengue to UKHSA; clinicians notify suspected malaria or enteric fever. A second infection carries a higher risk of severe dengue (Qdenga for people aged 4 and over who have had dengue, Green Book chapter 15a). Safety-net robustly.

knowledge.guideline: [1] UK malaria treatment guidelines 2016 (Lalloo et al., J Infect 2016) · [2] UKHSA: dengue guidance and Rare and Imported Pathogens Laboratory (RIPL) user manual · [3] UKHSA: Notifiable diseases and causative organisms: how to report · [4] Green Book chapter 15a: Dengue (UKHSA, October 2024) · [5] NICE NG253 Suspected sepsis in people aged 16 or over · [6] WHO Dengue guidelines for diagnosis, treatment, prevention and control, 2009 (international)
knowledge.summary: Fever in a returning traveller is malaria until proven otherwise, and one negative test does not exclude it: three negative samples over 24–48 hours are needed [1]. Fever, retro-orbital headache, severe myalgia and rash after South-East Asia fit dengue. Arrange same-day assessment, recognise warning signs, give fluids and paracetamol, and avoid NSAIDs and aspirin.

points.t: If malaria is suspected and the first film is negative, repeat after 12–24 hours and again after a further 24 hours; three negative samples over 24–48 hours make malaria unlikely [1]. In practice this means same-day hospital assessment, as films need an urgent laboratory.

Mosquito-borne flavivirus common in South-East Asia. High fever, severe headache with retro-orbital pain, myalgia and arthralgia, rash, nausea; often leucopenia and thrombocytopenia. Incubation is usually under 2 weeks, so symptoms starting over 2 weeks after return make dengue unlikely [2][6].
Dengue RT-PCR or NS1 antigen early in the illness, serology (IgM/IgG) later, via the local laboratory or RIPL [2]. Laboratories report confirmed dengue to UKHSA [3].

Abdominal pain or tenderness, persistent vomiting, clinical fluid accumulation, mucosal bleeding, lethargy or restlessness, liver enlargement, and a rising haematocrit with a rapid platelet fall. Severe dengue is most likely around the time the fever settles, often days 3–7 [6]. Any warning sign needs admission.

Malaria, enteric fever, hepatitis A, rickettsial infection, leptospirosis (freshwater exposure), chikungunya, HIV seroconversion, COVID-19 and influenza. Ask where, when, activities, bites, prophylaxis, food and water, freshwater, sexual and animal exposures.
Fluids, rest and paracetamol (dose per BNF). Avoid NSAIDs and aspirin because of bleeding risk. Screen for sepsis with NICE NG253 [5].

A second infection with a different serotype carries a higher risk of severe dengue. Qdenga can be considered for people aged 4 and over who have had dengue and plan to travel to a risk area [4]. Bite avoidance remains the main prevention.

model.text: Hello Aaron, I’m Dr Evans. What’s been happening?

I got back from Thailand four days ago and I feel awful. High fever, a pounding headache right behind my eyes, and aching all over, like my bones hurt. I’ve come out in a rash too. The walk-in did a malaria test and it was negative. What is it?
You sound really unwell, and I’m glad you got in touch. I’ll ask some focused questions about the trip and then go through the observations the walk-in centre recorded yesterday.
When did the fever start, relative to getting home?
A couple of days after I got back.
Where in Thailand were you: cities, countryside, jungle or islands? Did you get bitten much, and did you take any malaria tablets?
A few different places. I did get bitten. I’d have to check about tablets.
Any swimming in rivers or lakes, animal bites, new sexual partners, tattoos or anything like that? Any stomach upset?
model.why: Leptospirosis, rabies, HIV and blood-borne, enteric exposures

model.text: Nothing like that that I can think of.
Any tummy pain, being sick repeatedly, bleeding from your gums or nose, blood in your wee or stool, or new bruising or tiny spots?
No bleeding. I’m not being sick.
Any breathlessness, confusion, dizziness when you stand, or passing much less urine?
Not really. I’m drinking.
What have you taken for the pain?
Only paracetamol so far. I was going to get ibuprofen.
What have you been thinking this might be?
Some travel bug. The malaria test was negative, so I guessed not that.
What’s worrying you most?
Whether it’s serious. And I’m meant to be back at work.

I’ve got the walk-in centre’s observations from yesterday — your temperature, pulse, blood pressure, oxygen level and breathing rate. Have you checked your temperature today? Could you show me the rash on the camera, and press on it for me? And open your mouth so I can see your gums. (Febrile; recorded observations assessed against NICE NG253; rash seen on video, blanching; no bleeding from the gums.)

Here’s my thinking. The headache behind the eyes, the deep aching and the rash, after South-East Asia with mosquito bites, fit dengue, a virus spread by mosquitoes. But my first job with any fever after travel is malaria. One negative test doesn’t rule it out; it needs three over a day or two.
model.why: Leads with malaria and names dengue as the likely cause

model.text: So it could still be malaria?

It’s less likely, but I won’t guess. I’m going to send you to the hospital’s acute team today for repeat malaria tests, a blood count to check your platelets, liver and kidney tests, blood cultures, and a dengue test.
model.why: Same-day referral for films, FBC, LFT, U&E, cultures, NS1/PCR

model.text: If it is dengue, most people get better with fluids, rest and paracetamol. Please don’t take ibuprofen or aspirin. They can make bleeding worse if your platelets drop.
model.why: Supportive care; avoid NSAIDs and aspirin

model.text: Glad you said. How long will it last?
The fever usually lasts several days. The trickiest time is often when the fever comes down, so keep watching for warning signs even as you feel cooler. Fatigue can linger for a while after.
And work?
You’re not well enough to work this week, and I can give you a note if you need one. Dengue doesn’t spread from person to person in the UK in daily life, so it’s about you recovering.
Okay.
One for later: if this is confirmed, a second dengue infection can be more severe, so talk to a travel clinic before any trip to a dengue area. There’s a vaccine for people who’ve had dengue before.

While you wait for results: tummy pain, being sick and unable to keep fluids down, any bleeding, bruising or spots, feeling very drowsy or faint, or much less urine, go straight to A&E or call 999. Can you tell me what you’re going to do now?
Go to the hospital today for the tests, paracetamol and fluids only, no ibuprofen, and A&E if I get tummy pain, vomiting or bleeding.
Exactly. I’ll ring the team now and let them know you’re coming.

social.t: He is too unwell to work; offer a fit note after 7 days or self-certification before that.
Pre-travel advice and bite avoidance matter for future trips.

legal.t: Laboratories report confirmed dengue to UKHSA. Clinicians must notify suspected notifiable diseases such as malaria or enteric fever to the local health protection team (Health Protection (Notification) Regulations 2010).
Self-certify for the first 7 days; fit note thereafter if needed.

professional.t: Phone the admitting team; share the travel history, recorded observations and the negative walk-in test.
Another service’s negative test does not end the malaria question.

community.t: NaTHNaC and travel clinics for bite avoidance and dengue vaccine eligibility after confirmed infection.

redFlags: Any possibility of malaria: one negative test does not exclude it

ice: Idea: a travel bug; not malaria because the test was negative

playbook.diagnosis: “This is most likely dengue, a mosquito-borne virus, but malaria must be properly excluded today.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Dengue is like a severe flu passed on by mosquitoes. Most people recover with fluids and rest, but it can lower the cells that help blood clot, which is why we check your blood and avoid ibuprofen.”

management.reflectIce: “You thought the negative test ruled malaria out. It’s less likely, but one test isn’t enough, so we’ll repeat it today.”
management.psychosocial: Address work with a fit note and a realistic recovery time.
sharedPlan: Same-day hospital assessment: repeat malaria films, FBC, LFT, U&E, cultures, dengue NS1/PCR

Future travel advice; Qdenga eligibility after confirmed infection (Green Book ch 15a)
safetyNet: Abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding, bruising, drowsiness, faintness or little urine: A&E or 999
Warning signs can appear as the fever settles

pitfalls.intro: This station tests the returning-traveller reflex. Candidates fail by trusting one negative malaria test, by managing a febrile traveller at home, and by recommending ibuprofen.

items.fail: Accepting a single negative malaria test.
items.why: Three negative samples over 24–48 hours are needed (UK malaria guidelines 2016).
The differential depends on region, timing and exposures.
items.fix: Where, when, bites, prophylaxis, freshwater, sex, food and water.

items.why: Severe dengue often develops as the fever settles.
items.fix: Name abdominal pain, vomiting, bleeding, drowsiness; A&E if any.

items.why: It shapes whether he rests and returns if worse.
items.fix: Address it and offer a fit note if needed.

items.fail: Routine bloods with no same-day plan.
items.why: Fever after travel needs results today.
items.fix: Same-day hospital assessment with a phone handover.

professional.t: Phone the admitting team; share the travel history, recorded observations and the negative walk-in test.
Another service’s negative test does not end the malaria question.

community.t: NaTHNaC and travel clinics for bite avoidance and dengue vaccine eligibility after confirmed infection.

redFlags: Any possibility of malaria: one negative test does not exclude it
Dengue warning signs: abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding, lethargy, fluid accumulation
Postural dizziness or reduced urine output
ice: Idea: a travel bug; not malaria because the test was negative

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “This is most likely dengue, a mosquito-borne virus, but malaria must be properly excluded today.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Dengue is like a severe flu passed on by mosquitoes. Most people recover with fluids and rest, but it can lower the cells that help blood clot, which is why we check your blood and avoid ibuprofen.”

management.reflectIce: “You thought the negative test ruled malaria out. It’s less likely, but one test isn’t enough, so we’ll repeat it today.”
management.psychosocial: Address work with a fit note and a realistic recovery time.
sharedPlan: Same-day hospital assessment: repeat malaria films, FBC, LFT, U&E, cultures, dengue NS1/PCR
Fluids, rest, paracetamol (dose per BNF); no NSAIDs or aspirin
Future travel advice; Qdenga eligibility after confirmed infection (Green Book ch 15a)
safetyNet: Abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding, bruising, drowsiness, faintness or little urine: A&E or 999
Warning signs can appear as the fever settles

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station tests the returning-traveller reflex. Candidates fail by trusting one negative malaria test, by managing a febrile traveller at home, and by recommending ibuprofen.

items.fail: Accepting a single negative malaria test.
items.why: Three negative samples over 24–48 hours are needed (UK malaria guidelines 2016).
The differential depends on region, timing and exposures.
items.fix: Where, when, bites, prophylaxis, freshwater, sex, food and water.

items.why: Severe dengue often develops as the fever settles.
items.fix: Name abdominal pain, vomiting, bleeding, drowsiness; A&E if any.

items.why: It shapes whether he rests and returns if worse.
items.fix: Address it and offer a fit note if needed.

items.fail: Routine bloods with no same-day plan.
items.why: Fever after travel needs results today.
items.fix: Same-day hospital assessment with a phone handover.
